Explain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sidney Fisher).

speechtext:
This Bill provides for the appointment by the government of inspectors who may be called upon by the shipper or the receiver of closed packages of fruit to inspect it and mark its grade. At the present time we have inspectors, but their powers are limited to examining the fruit and stating whether it is falsely packed or not. That is of no commercial advantage. It is undoubtedly of great advantage in detecting false packing. I may say at the outset that when the Act was first proposed by the fruit growers, they wished inspectors to be appointed for the purpose of branding the apples, but they thought it would not be wise to encumber the Act with that provision at the beginning for fear of endangering its passage. Consequently they omitted to ask for it.
There are a great many advantages in having closed packages of apples or pears marked by a government inspector. It is hardly fair to ask the farmer, the fruit grower, or the packer to put on his goods a mark which may cause him to be fined. There is no other class in the community placed in exactly the same position. The Act, . when first brought into this House, did not provide that the packer must put on any particular mark. It provided that he ' may ' put on certain marks ; it was left optional. When the Act was in that position, there was no hardship. If a person put false marks on his barrels of apples, he knowingly took the responsibility on his own shoulders. But, the Act as amended last year provided that the farmer or packer must put on certain marks. If he thinks his apples are No. 1, and he puts on that mark, and they happen to fall below that standard and come under the notice of the inspector, he is liable to be fined. That is to say, the government compels the packer to put himself in a position where he is liable to be fined, which I think is not the case with any other class in the community.
By the amendment I propose, that onus would be taken off the packer. Under the present Act, the only way in which the packer can escape the onus is by marking his apples No. 2 or No. 3. I think three-fourths or nine-tenths of the apples packed last year were marked No. 2. Almost Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
any kind of apple may be marked No. 2, so long as the apples are the same all through the barrel, as there is no specification of that quality. Many of the apples thus marked were possibly No. 1, but the fact of their being marked No. 2 must to a certain extent have injured them on the market; yet the packer in many cases was afraid to mark his apples No. 1 lest he might subject himself to the penalties of the Act. I would not cancel the provision of the Act which provides for a No. 1 grade. I would rather have another provision defining the No. 2 grade; but I would take the onus off the farmer or packer of being compelled to mark his apples one or other of these grades, and I would provide that a sufficient number of inspectors should be appointed who, on the application of the packer, would take the responsibility of deciding whether his apples were No. 1 or No. 2.
It may be objected that this would cost a good deal. In my amendment I have not provided the method of payment; perhaps I should have done so. I do not for a moment propose that the government should take upon itself the cost of providing inspectors for every one who wants them ; but these inspectors would be paid as the inspectors of hides and the inspectors of many other commodities are paid, namely, by fees, made as low as would be consistent with covering the actual cost of the operation. When these fees are placed on the inspection, I am sure that there will not be an overwhelming quantity of apples to be inspected. I presume that nine-tenths of the apples that go forward are sold on consignment, and when they are so sold it is not absolutely necessary for them to be marked with any particular brand, as they are sold on their merits, and it must be a disadvantage to a man selling his apples in that way to feel compelled to brand them as No. 2. But there is a large quantity of apples, perhaps one-tenth or one-fifth of all those sold in this country, which are sold outright, by bargain sale-the way in which I think all fruit should be sold to ensure the seller getting the full value of it. If a government inspector could be called upon to mark these apples, see the position in which a farmer would be placed. A farmer has a quantity of apples to sell, and he grades them, and calls the inspector. The inspector marks them No. 1. The farmer immediately has a merchantable article which he can sell in Winnipeg or in the old country, or anywhere else. His apples have the standard brand of a government inspector, which is something of value to him, enabling him to place them on the market at their full face value, whereas at the present time he does not dare to mark them No. 1, but marks them No. 2, for fear he will overstep the mark and be fined.
The only objection which may be urged against this Bill is the cost of the inspec-

tion. I propose that that shall be paid by the farmer or the packer, so that that objection is removed. It may be said that to carry out the Act will require an army of inspectors. That will not be the case, however, because only a limited quantity of apples will require to be inspected. With proper management and care as many as a thousand barrels can be inspected in one day. I do not by any means, propose that the inspector should inspect every apple barrel, but that he should inspect the apples as they are inspected when sold in the old country-one in ten or one in twenty, as the case may be, of each brand or variety of apples. The apples may be opened up by men in the employ of the shipper, inspected by the inspector, and immediately closed up again by the shippers' employees, so that an inspector might easily in that way inspect a thousand barrels a day. It may be said that the inspection would be no guarantee of the quality of the apples, because the inspector does not inspect every barrel ; but that would be the well-understood condition of the sale-that only a certain percentage of the barrels were inspected. It would be a guarantee between the buyer and seller-whether between the farmer and the packer, or the packer and the merchant -that one barrel in every fifteen or twenty of these apples was inspected. So that 'i do not think that there is anything in the objection that this will be cumbersome. I cannot see any other valid objection why vre should not have an inspection of apples as of other commodities. We have an inspection of cheese and butter. When a man sends a cargo of cheese and butter to Montreal and there is a dispute, the inspector is called in and his verdict is binding. Why not follow' the same practice with regard to apples, which certainly require inspection just as much as butter and cheese ? We have hides inspected. A man cannot sell a hide unless it has been inspected by the government inspector. You wall find a government inspector in every city and town of the country, whose business it is to see that hides are properly examined and stamped. We have also an inspection of grain, though on somewhat different lines. This inspection of grain, as of many other goods, is paid for by the government, and costs many thousands of dollars annually ; but the inspection of fruit I do not propose to have paid by the government but by the people who ask for it. For my part, I cannot see any valid reason why this amendment should not be accepted. The fruit-growers are in favour of it. I wrote a number of prominent fruit-growers in different parts of the country, and in every case I was told that they fully agreed with me and were in favour of having this amendment put into our statutes. I wrote to Mr. A. H. Pettit, of Grimsby, who has always taken a leading part in all questions of legislation regarding fruit. Here is what he replied :
Your amendment is all right, but if I read Mr. Henderson's correctly it would annul the Inspection Act entirely. The great importance I attach to the inspection, is that being inspected and branded by the .inspector, it settles all questions as to the condition and quality, and we can never expect to make satisfactory contracts with the old country people unless wo can give them the guarantee (the inspector's brand). I have spoken to others and they all * approve of inspection and brand, with success to your amendment.
P.S.-Since writing the within, this thought strikes me. An Act for the prevention of fraud under which we are now acting is all right, but your amendment covers a more practical point. I want to sell, say 1,000 barrels of apples to an English firm, at a price f.o.b. I cannot ask that firm to accept draft unless I have some surety to offer the firm that I have fulfilled my part of the contract as to quality and condition, the inspector's brand settles that point, the all important point, sale by contract is far preferable than shipping to brokers.
I wrote Mr. McKinnon, who, ns the bon. minister knows, is another gentleman of high repute and standing, whose opinion Is respected by all who know him. He said :
Your own Bill I heartily approve, provided the buyer as well as the seller shall have the right to call for inspection and the party calling for it pays expenses.
Mr. Henderson's Bill is simply one to kill the Act in so far as it tends to make a distinct reliable Canadian brand.
I have here a letter from Mr. George Fisher. Mr. Fisher has been for years the inspector for the province of Ontario, and has always given the greatest satisfaction In his work. He is regarded by everybody as a man of good judgment. Here Is what he writes :
Yours of the 6th to hand. Your Bill providing for the official inspection of fruit is part of my contention, but I see no reason, if we pay for this inspection, which is quite right and proper, why inspectors should not be available to inspect any quantity large or small. I certainly think they should be, and this work should he done only at the request of the shipper and to serve his purposes alone, as when he requires a certificate in making a sale.
There are a number of other shippers who approve the principle of this amendment.
1 trust that the hon. minister will see his way clear to amend the Act on these lines. There are some other changes that may be made, but this strikes me as the most important.

I am very glad to have heard my hon. friend's remarks with regard to this amendment, because I was unfortunately absent when the Bill was first brought up. At that time my hon. friend the Minister of Finance asked that the Bill should stand until my return, and I have arranged with my right lion, leader the Prime Minister that an opportunity shall be given for its discussion. I have been thinking a good deal about this amendment and discussing it with a number of other peo-



pie. There are strong objections to it. The hon. gentleman has, to a certain extent, discussed some of those objections, but I would like to put them a little more forcibly and clearly than he has done. In the first place, while the hon. gentleman read one or two letters asking for an amendment of this character, he did not state that the Fruit-Growers' Association of Ontario had discussed this Bill and appointed a subcommittee to consider amendments to the Act, but that committee had neither passed any resolution nor asked for this or any other amendment to the Act. Various opinions were expressed, and a thorough discussion of all the provisions of the Act was had, yet the Fruit-Growers' Association could not agree on any recommendation regarding any amendment to the Act. In Nova Scotia the Fruit-Growers' Association also held a meeting and discussed the proposed amendment to this Act. They all agreed upon one amendment and one only, which they thought would be in the interests of the province. That amendment was not the present one. but was to the effect that No. 2 fruit should be defined. There is now only No. 1 or xxx defined, and other fruit-growers wanted the Act to go further and define No. 2 or xx as well as No. 1. Thus these two associations practically endorsed the Act as it now stands, and I do not see that because individuals here and there have objections to the Act as it now stands, while the representative bodies of fruit-growers do not believe and cannot agree upon this or any other amendment, with the one exception I have mentioned, we should make any serious change. My hon. friend has stated that the first Act os introduced did not contain this clause.
My hon. friend is mistaken in that. There was a Bill which did not become law, and which was only tentatively introduced in 1900. That, I believe, did not contain this clause C of section 4. But the Act as originally passed did contain the requirement that the grade of fruit shall be marked upon the package, and the amendment which made that stronger still in 1902 was simply an amplification or extension of clause 0 of section 4. My) hon. friend, however, must confess that this Act as it was introduced and adopted by parliament has always contained the requirement that the grade of fruit be marked upon the package. I confess that I consider this one of the essentials of the Act. I hold that if the packer is allowed to send forward a closed package without marking on it what it contains, he will escape to a large extent the wording of this Act, and the effect of the Act- which has been very good indeed upon the fruit trade of the country-will be almost nullified. I appreciate the fact that what the hon. gentleman lias said with regard to the particular section does not militate against the argument which he put forward for the adoption of this amendment, but still

speechtext:
I want to correct the statement he made with regard to the introduction at first of the Act. Now the hon. gentleman said that he wished to have the packer relieved from the onus of designating the quality of the fruit himself. But'it seems to me that this is essential to this Act. Nobody but the packer can really grade the fruit. It is true that, under the hon. gentleman's suggestion, the inspector can go and open 10 per cent of the packages and see what they contain. But this would not inform him as to what the other packages contained. He may easily light upon ten packages in a hundred which will grade No. 1 or x x x ; but there might be other packages very inferior, that he would not light upon. Under the hon. gentleman's suggestion, not only will all the fruit in such a case be designated ns of first quality, but the government's stamp will be put upon it, and the reputation of the department of the government of Canada will be pledged to the quality of the fruit) so stamped. Nobody can grade fruit in a closed package without first opening the package, except the packer himself; and it seems to me that it is proper and right, as well as the only safe way, that the packer should have the onus thrown upon him of packing his fruit honestly and marking it exactly for what he has put into the packages. The whole object of the Act is to protect the buyer from dishonest or negligent packing. Nobody except the packer can tell what is in the closed packages, unless the inspector opens every package. The hon. gentleman himself is well enough versed iii the trade to know that it would be impossible to open every package-and that he would be the first,-and all the trade would agree with him-to object to the inspector opening every package, to judge of its contents. This is in addition to the fact that it would be a practical impossibility, to find the army of inspectors necessary to carry out the work as designated by this amendment. The hon. gentleman says that, if a fee were charged, at first at any rate, very few inspectors would be called upon to inspect and grade fruit. I dare say that such would be the case, for one season. But if the buyers judge the fruit by its marks and consider the inspector's mark as a guarantee, you may be sure that they will very soon demand' that the government inspector's grade shall be given them and the mark of the government inspector be put upon all closed packages, and so sellers will be obliged whether they like it or not, in the interest of sales, to ask for this inspection. The result must be that it will require for this work an army of inspectors, at a certain time of the year, competent men well versed in the fruit trade and in fruit growing, who at that time of the year are specially difficult to find. Hast year, there were nearly 500.000 barrels of apples sent through the port of Montreal for export alone, to say nothing of the great number sold throughout

3S14
the country on local markets. This export trade is all rushed into, I suppose, less than three months of the autumn. And, for any number of Inspectors to be set to work to inspect and grade half a million of barrels of apples in the course of three months or less, to say nothing of the large number of the internal trade which is certainly as much if not double as much, would be almost a physical impassibility. The hon. gentleman says that, acting under his suggestion of inspecting 10 per cent of the packages, an inspector could inspect about a thousand a day. That is to say, they could inspect and know what was in one hundred packages, and they would mark nine hundred without-knowing what was in them. I do not think this is at all desirable. I know it was not what the House or the country expected or wanted when the Act was passed. I must say Also that, in the working of the Act no serious hardship, I believe, has arisen to justify this very material and essential change. Now, the hon. gentleman spoke of the onus on the packer, and said it was not right that the packer should have that onus thrown upon him, that, in fact, it was practically impossible for the packer to grade fruit correctly. I know that, during the last season a very large amount of fruit was sent forward as No. 2, because, unfortunately, the season was a bad one, and a very large proportion of the fruit was actually No. 2. But I doubt very much indeed if it could be substantiated that any fruit was sent forward which a packer believed to lie No. 1, and yet marked No. 2. It is quite contrary to the spix-it of the' trade to do so, and it is not at all necessary under the provisions of the Act; for, if the fruit is honestly packed as No. 1, the packer is perfectly safe in marking it No. 1, especially when, under the Act, a certain percentage of apples not quite up to No. 1 is allowed even, when the No. 1 mark is put upon the package. I think the packers can very easily live ill) to the Act by' honestly and correctly packing; and I think the public expect that of them. The purpose of the Act was to bring that about, and it has brought it about to a very large extent. I have had very satisfactory reports from the old country as to the packing of Canadian fruit during last season, and of the condition in which the fruit has reached the market. The people have declared distinctly that this is due largely to the operation of the Act. I cannot say' from memory' which paper it was in. but I saw the statement that not long ago. one of the associations of boards in England. had gone so far as to recommend to the United States the passing of such an Act as our Canadian Fruit Marks Act, because our Act has helped the fruit trade so much that it would be to the interest of people in the trade for the United States to adopt a similar law.
I venture to think that the amendment
which is proposed would to a large extent
120J
nullify the operation of the Act, and that there would be a serious danger both to the government and to the trade of the country; because I am satisfied that no government inspection could be as accurate and as careful as that of the packers themselves, and that if the government inspector were to make a mistake and, through neglecting to turn over every package, were to put upon some bad packages his stamp of No. 1 quality', it would affect the trade much more than if a private individual were to make a mistake and were to send forward fruit improperly marked. Of course, you may say that the government inspector must not make such a mistake. But the government inspectors, like other people, are liable to make mistakes, and especially would they be liable when they did not turn over more than a percentage of the fruit, and if they did not know what kind of fruit was jn more than a percentage of the number of packages which they were marking. Now the shipper himself, we will say, is making a reputation by the way in which he marks and packs his fruit. If the government steps in and takes that place, then ihe shipper himself is no longer responsible; if anything is found wrong he can shrug liis shoulders and say, it is not my fault. The result is that he loses that great benefit which any person gets who makes a reputation for himself over his own name. I think myself that the shipper's own guarantee is worth more to him-it may not be to the purchaser-but it is worth more to the shipper than any government guarantee could be. A government guarantee woujil be looked upon as impersonal, while the shipper's own guarantee, which is one of his own creation, is looked upon as personal to that shipper. If a man does his work well and honestly, he will make a reputation for himself and get a better price for his goods and a readier sale. All this will be taken away from him if the government inspector steps in. I do not feel, therefore, that I can accept this amendment.
I would say a word with regard to .the difficulty of operation under the amendment. If the hon. gentleman's proposal were carried out, and if every package was to be opened, I do not think the hon. gentleman himself, or those whom he professes to represent, would be satisfied with the result. If it were to be undertaken, it would be practically a physical impossibility to do it. The only way to carry out such an amendment as this, it seems to me, would be for the packer to employ a government inspector to come to his packing house and stay there during the whole tine of the packing season. That would mean a great expense to him, and lead to greater evils probably than the present condition of affairs can possibly create. Now the whole intention of the Act from the beginning was, not to have our fruit inspected, but it was clearly defined and stated here in the House

that it was meant to be a deterrent, it was meant to be a sword held over the dishonest or careless packer, to force him, by fear of the penalties attached to this Act, to do what he ought to be willing to do in his own interest, in the interest of the trade and in the interest of the reputation of Canada. The condition of affairs in this trade before this Act was passed, was such as to require some such action, and parliament in its wisdom adopted the Act as it stxvl, and changed it last session to make it more stringent in this particular section and in this particular respect. I am informed by those who have been watching the operation of the Act, that it.was not only good in the first place, but that the increased stringency of section 4 has made it still more beneficial. Under these circumstances, therefore, I cannot believe the amendment to be in the interest of the trade, or in the interest of the country, or even in the interest of the packers at large. There has been no general demand for this amendment from the representatives of the Fruit Growers' Association or from the packers ; and even if it were adopted, I cannot see how it could be carried out in such a way as to improve the facilities of the trade, and carry out the intention of the Act itself. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I must ask the House not to pass tlje second reading of the Bill.

Before the motion Is put, I desire to say a few words. I think the House, on consideration, would be in favour, if not of this amendment of my hon. friend from South Wentworth (Mr. Smith), at least of some amendment drawn on similar lines. I would say to the Minister of Agriculture that some of the fruit growers in the Niagara district find some objection to the present law in that there is no place, no locality where inspection can be expected to take place as a matter of course. My hon. friend from South Wentworth is moving in that direction in trying to get apples, to mention only that class of fruit, inspected where they are packed, or as near to the place where they are grown as possible, or to the place where they are packed and going to be shipped. I would point out to tlie Minister of Agriculture that there is no specified place where the inspection must take place. The inspectors go where they think the most apples are handled, they go to the large centres like Montreal, or Toronto, or perhaps Windsor.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE They go where they find the most fruit.

They want to do as much inspecting as possible. It would strike me, and has struck some of the fruit growers in the Niagara district, that if flic inspectors went where the fruit is grown, uot where it is taken off the cars or boats, but where it can be inspected before it is

shipped, they would strike equally large quantities. Supposing, for instance, thpy inspected at Hamilton, or Grimsby, or St. Catharines, or Winona, they would find as much fruit shipped in a day from these places as they would find in Montreal, that is to say, the inspectors would be exercising just as much economy of time in going to these towns I first mentioned when the apple shipping season is at its height. If they went to Winona, and then five miles further on to Grimsby, then sixteen miles further on to St. Catharines, they would find a very much larger number of barrels of apples or other fruit to inspect than by confining their operations to the larger cities. I think the Act requires some amendment in principle like this, providing some place where the shippers could be expected to have their apples inspected. I think the amendment of my hon. friend is in the right direction. It is much easier for men to look after their fruit at home, and it is reasonable that a fruit grower should expect his apples to be pretty well taken off his hands after they get upon the railroad. After he has shipped a great many barrels of apples, he has a lot of business to attend to, a large number of men under him, and it is natural that he would like to get rid of responsibility for his apples as soon as possible after they are shipped. When they get on the cars for Montreal, if they are going to England, he thinks his responsibility should cease. The minister may say that the fruit can be traced, that the fruit grower has an opportunity of knowing just as much as the railroad how many barrels he ships. For instance, if he ships on a railwa/, he knows by his bill of lading how many barrels they have in custody, and how many he can hold them responsible for, and I do not think it would be unreasonable that he should be able to know as to the quality. The government provides for an inspection which shall be .made somewhere, and I think it is better that it should be made as near as possible to the place where the goods are produced.

The government does not provide that the goods shall be inspected anywhere. There is no provision in the Act that any fruit shall be inspected. It must be shipped under certain conditions and it may be inspected to see if those conditions are complied with, but the government does not assume the responsibility of inspecting fruit.	.

Technically the Act may not provide for its inspection, but practically it is inspected by the government because an inspector is employed and the inspector prosecutes any person whose fruit is represented to be what it is not.
There are thousands of barrels that are never looked at.

The fruit-grower, if this Bill were passed, would be induced to bring about such a state of affairs that there would be a correct, proper and honest packing of fruit. We know that when the reputation of a certain place arises, when some man living at Grimsby, or St. Catharines, or Winona, or Burlington, succeeds in making a reputation for shipping good fruit, somebody else at the same place may get the benefit of that reputation because it is not the man's name that will be remembered so much as the name of the place where the fruit comes from. Where did this fruit come from ? It came from Grimsby, or St. Catharines, or Burlington, or Winona, or Guelph, or some other place, and that fact will probably have more weight with the purchaser than the name of the individual shipper. If the inspectors make an inspection, as we assume they will, being employed for that purpose, in order that the Act shall be properly enforced, I think the Bill of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) is in the right direction, because it would result in the inspectors making their inspection at the place where the goods are first packed. In regard to the number of barrels in each car that would have to be inspected, I do not think that any difficulty would be found in that. I do not know very much about it and I speak subject to correction, but I think that wheat is often inspected by the carload by government inspectors. They, of course, do not examine all the wheat in the car, but they examine samples taken here and there, and they form a pretty good opinion from such an examination. If a man packed a carload of apples and the inspector went through and took out a barrel here and there, I think we would be pretty safe in taking it for granted that he would be able to make a good inspection in that way. I do not think there would be anything unreasonable in making a regulation to that effect, as it would provide for such an inspection as the hon. member for Wentworth wants, and I think it would be a reasonable inspection without examining each barrel. As to the question of packing, of course, it is more or less a matter of opinion. If the inspector is where the apples are grown and lie differs from the shipper as to the classification it would be an easy matter to settle such a difference. The inspector says to the shipper:	You
must not put that fruit in as No. 1. The shipper asks :	Why ? The inspector gives
the reason. They would talk it over right there and one or other of them would have to give in. If the inspector were firm in his opinion the shipper would know what he must do with the next barrel, or next carload. or next season's crop of apples. It seems to me that it would he much easier to carry out the Act to secure the proper packing of apples if the inspector and shipper were brought in contact where the apples were being shipped. The hon. minister seems to think that a man's reputation would compel him to ship properly. That is all very well so far as it goes. But in many cases a man's reputation does not come quickly enough. The reputation of a fruit-grower, sometimes takes the best part of his business life to make, and it is desirable that he should be able to get the best price for his apples before he has made his reputation. It sometimes^ takes a man ten or fifteen years to make a reputation, because it sometimes takes him that time to learn how to produce the best fruit, and in another ten or fifteen years he may not have more than five or six good crops. If you wait until he has had enough good crops after he has learned how to grow the fruit properly to make a reputation, I am afraid the man will be ready to depart this life before that result has been achieved. I think he should get the benefit of the price that his apples are worth, if in the first year he is able to grow apples that are A No. 1. There is another matter that is not covered by the Bill which I do not think the hon. minister will object to me mentioning, although I am not prepared at present to move an amendment on that point. The present section 4 of the Act, as amended, provides that the shipper is entitled to mark a package containing fruit of the first quality No. 1, xxx, No. 2, xx, No. 3, x. Several fruit-growers in my part of the country have told me that they are satisfied that a fraud has been perpetrated upon them by some people they have shipped to. Unfortunately, they are not in a position to prove it because it is a fraud which is so easily committed. It is committed in this way :	A fruit-grower ships
a barrel of fruit marked xx, and the man to whom he ships takes a stencil and puts another x beside the original mark. The first purchaser sells these goods as being of first quality, or xxx. We, in the Niagara district, are satisfied that this has been done more than once. The person who is blamed in the cases in which this fraud has been detected, is the person who ships the fruit and who marked it xx. The shipper says : I only branded the fruit as xx, but the evidence is altogether against him. I think this practice would he made impossible if the shipper were only to mark upon the package the qualify in plain figures as No. 1, No. 2, or No. 3, and nothing else. These figures could not be altered, No. 3 could not be changed to No. 2, No. 2 could not be changed to No. 1, and there would be nothing which could be put beside the figure which would change the classification of the fruit. It would then not be so easy for the first purchaser to accomplish this fraud so as to get the benefit of selling fruit of a certain quality at the price of a better quality which he has been able to do without taking any risk himself. If he is caught he simply says : There is the barrel.

there are the marks upon it, go to the man who shipped the fruit. I think this suggestion is worth consideration.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me in regard to the last objection, that that might be remedied very easily by changing the kind of 'Stencil that the shipper uses. If he only leaves sufficient space to enable the proper number of X's to be put in, then, another could not be put there. In regard to the Bill before the House, I wish to say a word or two against it, because I do not see how it could be worked out if we were to have government inspectors of all fruit. I do not see how you could, under the present condition of affairs, authorize any one shipper to send word to an inspector that he must come at a certain time and go through a carload or a dozen carloads of fruit. It might occupy the time of one inspector for days or weeks while his services would be required in some other part. If the government is willing to take the responsibility and expense of sending a sufficient number of inspectors to inspect every barrel of fruit which is packed, then and not till then can we consider a provision of this sort. If the government is prepared to go to the expense of doing that, then this provision.would be workable, but otherwise it would not, and although I represent a fruit country, I rather hesitate to ask the government to go to that expense, because I think it would be unreasonable. Moreover the present Act is giving fair satisfaction throughout the country, and it has certainly accomplished a large measure of good. I believe that since the passage of the Act the fruit is better packed, and that a better reputation is being secured for our fruit in the foreign market.

I heartily endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade), because I believe it would be practically impossible to make this Bill workable, unless the government, intended to employ a very much greater number of inspectors than they have at present. This amendment to the Act would mean that the inspectors shall be at the call of the shipper whenever there is fruit that they think needs inspection, and that would entail the employment of an army of inspectors. There are other portions of the Dominion besides the counties of Lincoln and Wentworth from which apples are shipped, and it would certainly be very expensive to have inspectors at all these points. There is another feature in connection with it to which the hon. member for Lincolu (Mr. Lancaster) referred, and I think he was wrong on that point. He said that the reputation of the apple is known by the locality whence it comes, but 1 am of opinion that the brand of the fruit accounts for the reputation more than the locality. All the shippers have their own brands and they go on their merits in that way. It occurred Mr. LANCASTER.
to me that perhaps in the shipping season it might be advisable if the government could employ a few additional inspectors or sub-inspectors in certain localities, but if we make this Bill law it will be found to be impracticable to work it.

I wish to ask the Minister of Agriculture what is the practical operation of the Act at present. Is there an inspection of some portion of all the apples exported or used throughout the country. I suppose it means that only a few barrels, for instance, of a large ship meat would be inspected. If some of them are found not up to the mark what is the course pursued ? Do the inspectors in that case inspect every barrel. The Act does not seem to be of very much value unless that course is pursued, and yet if you do pursue that course you would require to do a very large amount of work in order to ensure any value whatever from the marks placed upon the apples by the shipper. If apples are not found to be up to the standard, are proceedings taken by the government against the packer or shipper or tlie person who is responsible.
I must reiterate what I have often said to the House : that this Act does not contemplate the inspection and grading of fruit by government inspectors.
I understand that perfectly. But it does to some extent propose to ensure that the marks placed upon the fruit by the shipper, are marks which can be relied upon by the consumer.

It does that by providing machinery for the working of the law, and penalties for punishment in case the barrels are improperly marked. The government have provided the machinery which any one can put in motion, and they have gone further and appointed certain inspectors so that shippers and packers would understand that in addition to the people to whom they were selling, there were also officials on the watch for infractions of the law. It is believed that the fact of having that machinery and having inspectors who are liable to drop on any shipment at any time, causes the packers to take more care in the packing and as to the marks they put on the fruit. I have figures here which have been submitted to the Committee of Agriculture by the gentleman who has charge of the work, and they show that last season the total number of barrels opened was 78,016 and the total number of boxes opened was 525. These were individual packages of shipments which aggregated 154,000 packages. The practice is that the officer of the department opens, say ten or fifteen packages out of a shipment of 100, and if he finds them good he

goes no further. If he finds them not up to the mark, he either condemns the whole lot as being similar to those he has opened, or, if the shipper wishes or requests it he examines the whole lot and grades Those that are good and those that are bad. That is the practice. I may say that we have four inspectors during the autumn in Montreal; two travelling inspectors in Ontario; three inspectors in the maritime provinces ; one in British Columbia and one in Manitoba. It is quite understood that these men cannot possibly deal with more than a percentage of the packages and the whole intention of the Act is deterrent; not necessarily to catch them but to induce them to act honestly through the danger of being caught. Generally when a first offence is detected the persons are warned, and if the offence is repeated they are prosecuted, and so far we have not failed in any prosecution we have undertaken. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) referred to a case where the first purchaser changed the mark by adding another x. There was no difficulty in proving that offence, and the first packer was exonerated. and the seller who changed the mark was punished. There is no great difficulty in making proof of that kind, but nevertheless the first packer ought to make such a mark that it cannot be easily changed. If a ring were put around the original two xx the third x could not very well have been added, and the stencil is usually made with a ring around. I am sorry that some packers do not use stencils which are difficult to change, and if they are so careless 1 am not sure that they ought to be protected from their carelessness. Stencilling is so cheap and easy that I would not care to change the Act so as to protect those who are so indifferent as merely to mark with a blue pencil on the package. IIow-ever, I may say that we have encouraged the use of the marks Nos. 1, 2 and 3, and I am glad to know that that encouragement is bearing fruit, and that a great many packers throughout the country are using these marks instead of the old ones, and I hope that before long the Canadian fruit trade generally will use a uniform system of marks.
Does the minister think it necessary to have the x marks as well as those ?

That was allowed in deference to a section of the country in which the x marks were largely used ; but I am glad to say that the Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are being largely used instead of the x marks. With regard to the locality of the fruit and the use of personal marks, I may say that in a great many instances the packer uses his personal mark, though the fruit comes from ten or a dozen different localities. I am sure that my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) buys fruit all over the province of Ontario and puts his name on it. Though the localities from which the fruit comes are not known, Mr. E. D. Smith is known. That is the reputation which I had reference to having been built up by my hon. friend.

May I be allowed a word more, with the consent of the House, with reference to the matter alluded to by the minister-the case in which the packer had changed the brand ? There was a case of that kind in my own county, in which the tine imposed was merely nominal; and the general opinion of the fruit growers and packers throughout the country was that the tine was entirely inadequate to the offence.
I think the fine for an offence of that kind ought to be ten times greater than for the other offence.

There is one particular in which the Act places the apple dealer at a disadvantage. It is this. There are men who, like the hon. member for Wentworth, buy thousands of barrels of apples on the trees. They then employ men and boys to grade these apples and pack them, and the Act holds the man who buys the apples responsible for these packers. If the apples are not properly packed, he is fined, and his name is sent broadcast through the country ns that of a man who has been fined for fraudulently packing apples. If I were a shipper of apples, I would send them out under the second grade, and would work out my own reputation, as suggested by the hon. member for Lincoln. I think the government, in their care to have apples properly packed and sent forward, so as to ensure a good name for this country, should not have gone any further than to require a barrel of apples to be packed uniformly from the top to the bottom, leaving people to put on their own marks. If the apples were found to be not uniformly packed in the barrel from the top to the bottom, then impose as heavy a fine ns you please.

I want to ask the hon. minister a question. I stated that the Act at present compels a man to put on the grade mark, whereas the Act as originally introduced into the House in 1900 did not do so. I understood the minister to say that I was mistaken. If so, I would like to have my mistake pointed out.

No. I said that the Bill as originally introduced in 1900 did not contain that clause, whereas the Bill as introduced in 1901, when it was made law, did contain it, in section c of clause 4. The Bill introduced in 1900 was only a tentative Bill, and was not even discussed.
Motion negatived, on division.

In the absence of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), I beg leave to move that Bill (No. 130) to amend the Fruit Marks Act, 1901, be now read the second time. The purport of this Bill is simply to abolish the designations and grades of markings in the Act. The objections urged by the fruit growers to the Act in that respect are so well set forth in a resolution passed by the Fruit Growers' Association at Burlington, that I cannot do better than read it. The purport of it is as follows
Noticing that Bills to amend the Fruit Marks Act are being introduced in the House ot Commons. many fruit growers consider it an opportune time to draw the attention of legislators and the public to some grievance which exist under the Act, and possibly to suggest remedies for some of these evils.
No one questions the fact that great improvement in the packing of fruit has resulted from the passing of the Act of 1901. As far as known all fruit growers are in the fullest sympathy with what was ostensibly the purpose of its designers. The purpose of the Act as clearly stated and understood at a conference between the Hon. the Minister of Agriculture and representative fruit growers and dealers was- so to frame it as to consider the interests of the growers in preference to those of the dealers when these interests conflicted :-
To prevent fraud in packing by having the contents of ail closed packages to correspond fairly with the face or shown surface of such package.
To give the packer's name and address in full as a guarantee of good faith.
And to stipulate that certain marks to be defined were not to he used unless the contents of the package graded up to a certain standard, all other marking to be at the discretion of the shipper.
These provisions would have adequately protected the public from fraud, would not have been onerous on the grower or shipper and would have been entirely acceptable to the great majority of fruit growers and to fair minded dealers.
The beneficial results have been derived principally from section 7 of the Act, which provides that the face of any package shall be a fair representation of the contents, and from clause * A' of section i which provides for the name and address of the packer being ' placed on all packages. These are the vital points in the Act and constitute within themselves a sufficient safeguard for the public, and with the penalties imposed for infractions a sufficient deterrent to such packers as may be fraudulently inclined. These demands are not too much to expect of the ordinary fruit grower, who can readily understand the difference between honest and fraudulent packing and who cannot but understand the importance of fruit going forward under his name having a uniformity of excellence.
These improvements in the trade and satisfactory conditions, as before stated, have been effected entirely under certain sections of the Act as originally passed in 1901, but in the dying hours of the session of 1902 amendments to the Act were railroaded through the House without explanation or due consideration, and being quite uncalled for either by the public or the fruit grower. The objectionable feature of these amendments are principally embodied in Hon. Mr. FISHER.
clause ' C ' of section 4, which arbitrarily demands that a farmer shall grade to a specified standard which must necessarily vary materially in different sections, and in the ideas of various individuals, and then brand with a fixed mark to designate the grade or quality, which uo other class of the community is called upon to do and to which no class but the farmer would submit.
It is therefore widely regarded as an unwarrantable interference with the fruit growing industry and with the rights of a citizen, and the farmers of the Dominion should as one man raise a protest against this injustice being perpetrated on a section of their calling and resent the indignity thus thrust upon them.
Penalties are provided for failing to comply with all the conditions required and heavier penalties for attempting to do so when the judgment of the farmer fails to conform to that of the inspector, although it may be the judgment of an experienced and honest packer against that of an inspector whose efficiency is questionable, and the farmer is at'once branded a criminal without the privilege of trial by jury. Thus trade is seriously hampered by terrorizing the grower who, rather than take the risk of marking his packages, and incurring the odium of being fined, is induced to sell his fruit to the speculator much below its value or allow it to remain in the orchard.
This compulsory grading and branding is not only impossible as applied to all packers under varying conditions but it is both absurd and useless. Being the marks of the owner who is an interested party, those marks demanded by the Act would not be considered by any court and would consequently have no commercial value in case of a dispute between buyer and seller.
There .should be no compulsory grade marks, and responsibility for grades should not rest on the farmer but on qualified and competent inspectors, who should be available to do inspection work when required, and issue certi-cates as in other lines of business-these certificates would be final in case of dispute as to quality.
The Act might in the opinion of many shippers define No. 2 or No. 3 fruit, but it should be entirely optional with a shipper whether he has his fruit graded to a government standard or not. Millions of bushels of wheat change hands annually without inspection, and when it is inspected the owner does not Indicate the quality, but the inspector makes his examination and issues his certificate. In such cases the person requiring the services of the Inspector pays the established fees.
I cannot put the case plainer than it is put in this circular. Under the Act a packer is compelled to put certain marks on his barrels. The hon. minister has told ns that in the Act of 1901, there is a similar condition. I cannot see it. Section G describes a brand called A No. 1 Canadian brand apples. and section 7 describes No. 1 Canadian brand, and provides and the Act provides that any one who uses these brands must conform to certain specifications. No one. however, is obliged to use these brands. That is what the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) complains of. and his Bill wipes out the grades altogether. 1 would not go so far. I would like to see these grades in the Act, but only as they were in the Act first introduced. I would like

to liave two grades exactly defined, but to have the.branding of these grades optional. Let the packer not be obliged to put on these marks and thus avoid subjecting himself to a fine if he makes a mistake. The trouble with the present law is that a, packer has to put certain marks on the apples without being in a position to know whether the packing corresponds to these1 marks or not. and he thus may render himself innocently liable to a fine. The hon. minister's objection that the inspection would cost too much is not reasonable. When a car is examined, every barrel is not inspected, but only some of the barrels. If you take one barrel out of a lot of one variety, packed in the one orchard, it is fair to assume that the remainder of the barrels will be the same. The Act is an excellent one in many respects and has done a great deal of good, but it lacks some things to make It perfect. There are three things wanting. first, grade No. 2 should be defined; second, the marking of these grades should not be compulsory; third, the inspector should be appointed at the instance of any one requiring him. Suppose a car of apples is refused on its arrival. An inspector is called in, and h,e may go or not as he likes. If he happens to be on hand, and does go and examine a few of the barrels, what may be the consequence ? The shipper may be asked to lose fifty cents or a dollar a barrel on the whole cargo when the inspector has only examined five or six barrels. That, according to the hon. minister's contention, is not fair, because five or six barrels would not indicate what the cargo is like, and consequently the shipper has no right to lose. Of course I know that the inspection would not hold as evidence in a court of law, but nevertheless any one can understand that when a shipper goes into court and the evidence of the inspector is taken, the verdict is likely to go against him. I do not know but that the inspection would be absolutely just if it were taken on each of the different brands in the car, but if only taken on five or six barrels which happened to be shoved to the front and were picked out as the worst barrels and then the whole cargo condemned, one can see the injustice. But if the apples had been examined before shipment, and it was then found that they were not up to grade, the shipper could either repack them or sell them as grade No. 2, instead of grade No. 1, for which he would get within twenty-five cents of No. 1. But once the apples are shipped and received by the consignee, and condemned on the examination of a few barrels by the inspector, as not being up to the grade mark, the shipper has to take whatever he can get, because it would not pay him to go to law. Instead of being a benefit as it might be, if made before the apples were shipped, the inspection becomes a detriment. Suppose a shipper sends his apples to Winnipeg or Montreal, and on arrival they are condemned, he is in no position to remedy what he might have done very innocently, because in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, the packer gets the best apples he can, but they may not be put up all right. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, as the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. (iilmour) pointed out, the packer gets men to pack the apples. He gets the best men he can, but if they do not put them up right, according to his judgment, still, he is at their mercy to a great extent. The hon. minister knows that very well. When the apples reach Montreal or some distant place, he may be notified that they have not been properly graded and he is then in no position to save himself. If his apples were condemned at home, he could re-pack them and get what they are worth out of them. There are many other things to be said on this subject, and I trust that other members will take up this discussion. I feel that we rest under a grievance as things are at the present time.

I understand that we are now discussing the Bill standing in the name of the hon. member for I-Ialton (Mr. Henderson). It seems to me that the argument of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) was, to a certain extent, mixed up with his argument for his own Bill. While I would not presume to reflect in any way upon the clearness of what he has been saying, I must confess that I have been a little at a loss to know whether' he has been speaking in favour of his own Bill or in favour of that of the hon. member for Halton. However, I may follow his example ; and I would like to quote against the Bill now before us what the hon. gentleman read in favour of his own Bill. He read two or three letters in which remarks were made about the necessity of having the inspectors go to the orchards and there inspect the fruit. But he read other sentences from these same letters which stated distinctly that the amendment jiroposed by the hon. member for Halton, if passed, would completely destroy the efficacy of the Act. I agree with those statements. I think that if this amendment were passed, the Act would be emasculated to such an extent as to be of very little use. Now, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) referred back to the Bill of 1901. I have not at the moment that Act under my hand. I understood that when the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Smith's) own Bill was being disposed of, and the hon. member for Halton not being present, we would not take up his Bill, so I sent my papers away. Speaking from memory of the Bill of 1901, it did not specify any particular marks, but it did require the designation of the grade contained in the Act of 1901, which are now part of the law, but it did specify in part that the grade of the fruit should be marked upon the pack-

age. That was and is an essential of the Act. If the packer is allowed to pack his fruit and not mark upon the package the quality of fruit, it would be impossible to hold liim to any penalty under the Bill. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) bows his head. Is that the object-to prevent the packer being pursued and punished for improper packing and false marking ? If it is his object, I take issue with him squarely, and say that the country wants the packer to be pursued and punished for bad packing and false marking, and that that is the very object of the Act. I do not think the hon. gentleman really wants the Act so emasculated that the packer shall escape all responsibility. I do not think the hon. gentleman would take the responsibility before his constituents of saying that he wants to emasculate the Act in that way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: How is the hon. minister going to reach the packer, when he is really employed by the buyer of the apples ?
I would inform the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gil-mour) that the man who actually packs the fruit is responsible, and, under the Act, is liable to a penalty as his employer is.
But you cannot find him. How then can you fine him ?

Exactly. That is why we want to get at the employer. You cannot find the poor man who has been paid $1 a day to pack the apples-he may be a hundred miles away. But if we found him and punished him, that would not be of any use. We look to the employer, who is a responsible man and responsible for the working of his employees. That is essential to the Act, and I think the House and the country want that to remain a part of the law. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) himself would like to see the employer relieved of the responsibility. If this were done, the Act would not be worth the paper it is printed on. If the hon. member for Wentworth employs men to pack fruit and can throw the responsibility for bad packing on these men, how could he be held responsible or be punished for the bad packing of the fruit ?
The hon. minister is quoting me wrongly-
I am speaking of the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour).

But I am referring to what was said before the hon. member for East Middlesex spoke. I made no reference in what I said to the packer escaping responsibility.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE No; but the hon. member for East Middlesex did. I said that the hon. member for Wentworth would not wish the packer to Hon. Mr. FISHER.
be allowed to evade responsibility. He knows that the employer ought to be responsible, for he is the only person who can be successfully pursued. The workman who is employed at $1 a day cannot be pursued. It is true that if he does bad packing he is liable to a fine, as his employer is. But if we could pursue him only, the Act would not be of any. use. It is the employer who must be looked to and held responsible. The hon. member for Wentworth sells his fruit under his own name. When I buy a barrel of apples marked ' E. D. Smith ' I expect to get something good, for the hon. gentleman's reputation, position and standing are back of all he does. But if I turned to John Jones, employed by Mr. E. IX Smith to pack fruit in his orchard and tried to hold him because a barrel of apples I bought was not equal to the markings, I should stand but a poor chance. The hon. gentleman does not Wish the buyer to be put in that position, I am sure. He does not tvnnt to shirk responsibility, nor does he believe that the employers of labour wish to shirk responsibility. Their reputation is made by being responsible, by giving a guarantee for the fruit they pack and ship under their name. But what I was saying, and what the hon. member (Mr. Smith) misunderstood me about, was in regard to clause C of section 4, which was originally in the Act as passed by this House. In the session of 1902 there was an extension of clause C of section 4, specifying certain markings which had to be put upon the package. That was done to secure uniformity of markings, but the clause is no more stringent in requiring the designation of grade to be put upon the package than was that of 1901.
If the hon. minister will permit me
Yes.
I cannot see how the minister can argue in that way. The original Act did not compel any man to put any particular mark on the package.

The hon. geutleman will excuse me. Here is the Bill of 1901, section 4 :
Every person who by himself or through the agency of another person packs fruit in inclosed packages intended for sale, shall cause the package to. be marked in a plain and indelible manner before it is taken from the premises where it is packed :
(a) With the initials of the Christian names and the full surname and address of the packer ;
(h) Both the name of the variety or varieties ; and
(c) With the designation of the grade of the fruit.
That is the Act of 1901. It contains clause c.

Yes. That is not the Bill as proposed, it is the law that passed, and in 1902 an addendum was made to that clause which required that in making the designation of the grade of the fruit, certain marks should he used, namely, x, xx and xxx, or No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3. That is an addendum to the clause ; hut the essential of the clause, that the grade of the fruit has to be put upon the package, was contained in the original law.
I was referring to the Bill that was introduced at the suggestion of the Fruit Growers' Association.

That was introduced in 1900, but after further discussion with the fruit growers, with the dealers, and with the packers, and after full consideration in committee, that Bill was drawn up and introduced in 1901, and the designation of the grade of the fruit was required, and it was passed in that form by this House, after thorough discussion in which the hon. gentleman himself took part.

I think this amendment destroys to a large extent the original intention of the Act. As stated by the Minister of Agriculture, in the Act of 1901, clause c, of section 4, merely says that the barrel or package shall be marked with the designation of the grade of the fruit Then section G forbids any person to sell, offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, any fruit improperly marked. This was found not to be definite enough in operation, hence the Act of 1902, which states in subsection c that the packages should lie marked :	[DOT]
*With a designation of the grade of fruit, which shall include one of the following six marks : for fruit of the first quality, No. 1 or XXX ; for fruit of the second quality, No. 2 or XX ; and for fruit of the third quality, No. 3 or X.
Then it urns necessary to amend section 0 in consequence. Now the amendment before the House proposes t >
sweep away everything that was done in 1902 and leave it to the general expression that there shall be a designation of tlie grade of the fruit, leading to the same uncertainty that existed before. I think that would be very unwise. In my judgment the only amendment that is needed in this Act is the one that has been asked for by the fruit growers and shippers of the maritime provinces, namely, that not only should there be a specification of the variety of No. 1 or xxx, hut there should also be a specification of the varieties Nos. 2 and 3, so that a party should be fined for improper packing of those varieties just the same as in the case of other varieties. I think, therefore, it would be a mistake to do anything which would lead us
back to tlie uncertainty that has existed. No Act of this kind can he framed and put into successful operation from the start. It requires some experience. I think that the amendments passed in 1902 were based entirely upon the experience of those who had been endeavouring to operate tlie Act.
1	am sure that so far as the growers and shippers of the lower provinces are concerned, this Act is popular as it stands, and that the only amendment it requires is one with regard to this specification.
As I understand the present Act, it only applies to fruit marked No. 1, and not to the other grades.

It provides for them, hut it does not describe them. I am in sympathy with the proposal of my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade), and the hon. member for Wentworth himself stated a few minutes ago that he was in favour of having No.
2	grade defined. I think the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) will find that there is a special clause describing what must he put into a package marked No. 1, but there is no clause describing what must he put into a package marked No. 2 or No. 3, and it is that definition which the fruit growers of Nova Scotia and the hon. member for Wentworth have proposed. I am in sympathy with the idea, hut I have not yet prepared an amendment to the Act. If I think best, before the end of the session, I may do so.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question before the Chair is clause 1, of section 3, and the amendment of Mr. Barker to include railways in the operation of the Act.
Amendment (Mr. Barker) negatived.
On section 3, subsection 2 :
Any section of this Act may, by any special Act passed by the parliament of Canada, be ex-c:f pted from incorporation therewith, or may thereby be extended, limited or qualified. It shall be sufficient, for the purposes of this subsection, to refer to any section of this Act by its number merely.

Surely we have that power at any time in the future without putting it in this Bill ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. I suppose there is no objection to that phraseology. We are following the present Act in putting it in. We have the power, no doubt, but tliere is no harm in stating that it is intended to be of universal

I could understand that in a special Act which 1ms already become the law in the Dominion, but it refers to future Acts of parliament that may be passed. It means that a person might make an application for a charter and yon reserve the power to the Dominion of Canada to pass an Act which may exempt that special charter from any clause of this Bill.
We are providing for application to Acts which are passed. They are covered by this sub-clause and this subclause qualifies the first sub-clause of the section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
-that is from incorporation under this Act, -or may thereby be extended, limited, or qualified. It shall be sufficient for the purposes of this subsection, to refer to any section of this Act by its number merely.
If you are passing this Bill in the sense you are supposed to ba passing it, I think if there is one thing above another that we should look after it is the certainty that it shall apply to all railways and that we should not be delegating our powers. I have every confidence in this House as it is at present constituted, but we are doing a very serious thing and we are doing more than at first sight may be supposed. We are saying that notwithstanding the fact that we are creating a commission to dispose of the matters that are said to be creating so much trouble in the country-that a commission is necessary, any railway company may receive a charter by special Act exempting it from the provisions of this Bill, and that if the Railway Committee recommend the granting of such a charter it will be passed because in the House the onus is usually laid upon any person who objects to make a strong case in opposition to the report of the Railway Committee. It is dangerous legislation in connection with a Bill whose application is supposed to be universal. It is true that we have been told it is not the Intention of the government that it shall apply to government railways but it is universal except that it does not apply to government railways. If it does not apply to all the railways of the Dominion it is no good. This is legislation to create a Railway Commission to look after those matters which are supposed to be creating so much trouble in the country that a commission is necessary to deal with them, and if it does not apply to all railways there does not seem to me to be of very much use-in passing this law. This subsection is an invita-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
tion to this parliament, or to the next parliament, or to any parliament, or to Railway Committee in any year to pass a special Act incorporating the railway and exempting it from the provisions of this Bill That is the elfect of it. The hon. minister may say that parliament would not do anything that was not wise. I do not think we should pass legislation that would imply that it might do so I think the Bill would be much better if that subsection were not in. The Bill would still fulfil all its purposes. It would not impair the strength of the Bill itself. This is not in the old Railway Act. I have compared the old Act with this Bill, and there is no such section as this in it. There is a section in the old Act which says :
This Act, subject to any express provisions of the special Act, and to the exception hereinafter mentioned, applies to all persons, companies and railways within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, except government railways.
This subsection does not help to carry out the Bill at all. It cannot strengthen the Bill or make it more easy to work. Unless there is some better reason than that which has been advanced, I think we should strike that subsection out.

Does it not seem to the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals that this subsection is useless ? It simply enunciates a principle that does not require to he stated in the Bill. There is no doubt that the party who drafted the Bill thought it necessary to have this subsection 3 preceded by a recital as in subsection 2, but it seems to me that the subsection is useless and as the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. All'. Hag-gart) says may encourage parties seeking special charters to have these 'charters excepted from the operation of some useful section of this Bill.

I must confess that I cannot see this matter in the way in which it has presented itself to the minds of my hon. friends opposite. I cannot see there is the slightest fault in the subsection, but I see every advantage in it. This is certainly no more an invitation to parliament to introduce special exceptions into special Acts which may be passed hereafter than is the existing law which says :
This Act, subject to any express provisions of the special Act, and to the exception herinafter mentioned, applies to all persons, companies and railways within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, except government railways.
That is what the old law says, and I cannot see any harm in It. Parliament will exercise its discretion, as it must have the right to exercise its discretion, as to whether in any case it will make any special enactment varying from the general enactment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If this parliament can always do it, what is the use of telling them in this Act that they can do it. It is no argument to say that this clause has always been in the law. Why, that is more Tory than I am. You practically say that because it always has been, it always shall be.
I should be sorry to assume that everything in the existing Act requires to be amended. It must be remembered that this Act is not an Act simply for the purpose of creating a railway commission.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We are discussing here a public Bill containing a broad general principle that the commission shall have jurisdiction over all railways except two, and yet in the sub-clause we provide that an Act creating a particular company hereafter may contain a clause detracting from the general principle we settle on here. There is a great deal to be said for the argument that the principle of a Bill of this important character should not be subject to be altered by some private Act.

This Act provides for a great variety of things such as the construction and alterations of lines, railway crossings, protection required on railways, and hundreds of other different things. When parliament created the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to deal with all these matters it deemed it advisable that they should exercise their power under the Railway Act, subject to the provisions of any special Act that might be passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We should have a little better explanation from the minister. I am trying to help to make reasonable legislation out of this, and although I do not pretend to know as much railroad law as the minister does, yet I think that all he says he wants to do by this clause is done by the constitution without any such clause as this at all. It is safe to say that any particular Act of the parliament of Canada can exempt itself from the operation of this Act without this clause being in at all. As to the argument of the minister, I would say that the more things there are for a special Act to interfere with, the more dangerous it is to invite them to interfere by such a clause as this. Even on the minister's own argument this clause should be struck out. I appeal to the Minister of Justice if I am not right, that without this clause at all any special Act of the parliament of Canada would have the effect which this clause says it shall have. I say it is bad legislation to put in words which are mere surplusage, and which would leave doubt in the minds of the judges who would be construing this clause as to what the intention of the parliament of Canada was in passing such a law. According to the intention of the promoter of the Bill there are five lines here which are absolutely unnecessary, and I say that it is bad draftsmanship and mere confusing surplusage to pass such a law. I wish that some one more eloquent that I am could impress upon the Minister of Railways and Canals the necessity for striking out this sub-clause.

I am not a lawyer, but it appears to me that the legislation of this House should be drafted so that a man of common sense can understand it. I cannot help but draw attention to the fact that I have heard in this House from the Minister of Justice and other members of the government the expression :	what
do you mean by this legislation ? Not long since the Minister of Justice put that question in one of the committees. Would it not be better rather than to have such crude legislation passed by the parliament of Canada, that some person should be paid who would be able to bring common sense into the drafting of a Bill so that we would know what the language means ? What is the use of passing legislation in this House with reference to which the Minister of Justice, who is supposed to have the brightest intellect in the House has to ask what it means? Should not a Bill be so drafted that the trained intellect of legal gentlemen can tell what it means when we put it on the statute-book? How can we expect the judges of the land to construe such legislation when even the Minister of Justice does not know what it means ? It appears to me that it .would be better for the Minister of Railways and Canals to bring common sense to bear on this legislation. Can we not have a clause here, founded on common sense so that the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways and Canals will know what it means ? I am willing, as the representative of a rural constituency, to pay a man who is skilled in drafting legislation. It may appear to be a frivolous subject to some hon. gentlemen, but I feel serious about it. Perhaps these hon. gentlemen want to make a little money out of the legislation when it comes before the courts ; but I want our legislation to be so plain that a wayfaring man, though a fool, shall not err therein ; and I am willing to pay from the exchequer of Canada a gentleman who is skilled in drafting legislation, so that when it is placed on the statute-book we shall know what it means.

It appears to me that the following words might be left out of this section :
Any section of this Act may, by any special Act passed by the parliament of Canada, be excepted from incorporation therewith, or may thereby be extended, limited, or qualified.
These words appear to me. as a layman, to be unnecessary, because they give us no power that we do not possess already. Perhaps I am not right in my interpreta-

tion of them, but that is the way they appear to me.
