speechtext:
We have to look at this Act in the interest of the people, as to how it may be construed. In my humble opinion it is very dangerous legislation to Put any language into an Act which is not necessary; because, although we are legislators making the law, the judges in construing it do not go by what we may say here, or by consulting 'Hansard,' but they go by well known legal principles of construction. If a case arose under this Act, and an argument were made by counsel on one side and on the other, the court would be almost constrained to say :	We must
give a different effect to the Act from what we would if that subsection were not there. If the minister could state any special reason why he is putting this language into the Bill, if he could show that it made the Bill mean something that it would not mean if this language were not there, I could understand it being there; but if it only means what would be the case even if the language were not there-simply that a special Act can, if it is necessary, in the opinion of parliament, at the time it passes that special Act, override this general Act-if that is all that is meant, then I do not see the use of these words being here at all. If we put this in, the courts may feel bound to give special effect to every word, phrase and sentence in the Act, and will conclude that parliament meant something else than would have been the law if this were not in and therefore different to what we intend.

Section 3 provides :
This Act shall apply to all persons, companies ana railways, other than government railways within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and shall be incorporated and construed as one Act, with the special Act, subject as herein provided.
It does not say it shall apply absolutely, but it shall apply ' subject as herein provided.' Therefore you cannot leave out sub-Mr. SPUOL'LE.
sections two and three, unless you strike out ' subject as herein provided.'
Subsection three makes that perfectly clear. You will have a complete section without subsection two being in at all. I am only proposing to strike out subsection two.
I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he would strike out subsection 2 and make subsection 3 subsection 2 ?
Yes.

Yes, that was my intention ; and I may say to the committee that this section as a whole has been very carefully considered, and has been gone over and over and talked about a good deal. It does, in a measure and to the extent which I shall state in a moment, vary the old third clause. Now, let me point out that the main portion of the section, the first subsection, could not very well be left standing alone and declaring on the face of it that this Act shall apply to all the railways within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. You would have to recognize, as a matter of fair notice to everybody trying to interpret the law, that there might be within the four corners of the special Act exceptions which would override similar or correspondinar clauses and sections of this Bill. That is fair drafting, it seems to me, and we cover the point by stating :
This Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways (other than government railways)

within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and shall be incorporated and construed as one Act with the special Act subject as herein provided.
And what is that ?
Any section of this may, by any special Act passed by the parliament of Canada be excepted from incorporation therewith, or may thereby be extended, limited, or qualified.
That is, it is not left merely to implication as I read the clause. Parliament, in a special Act would except from the operation of the general law any one clause or clauses that it chose to so describe and so declare. Well, it is not a complete answer to the propriety of putting it in here to say : Well, parliament has the power to put it in any way. Proper and usual drafting would rather impel one to put in just such a clause as that. Then, we come to the third clause, which deals -with the case of special Acts heretofore passed. Now, the old section 3 provides :	.
This Act, subject to the express provision of the special Act

That conveys, as my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) lias very properly said, the idea that parliament contemplated that special Acts would be passed which would vary the provisions of this Act, and deem it advisable to so enact that one will see at once it speaks in general terms of the| special Act. That special Act might be a special Act of the parliament of Canada or it might lie a special Act of one of the provincial legislatures. For we are frequently in the habit of declaring some special work constructed under some local incorporation, a work for the general advantage of Canada. ; That is one of tlfe difficulties we had to face in creating this Act, but we have all sorts of provisions in the local Acts entirely at variance with tlie\ General Act, and the question is whether we have by the general nature of these Acts made these special Acts part of the law of Canada and thereby withdrawn the case from the operation of the General Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I sympathise with the minister's views to a certain extent, and in criticising the Act, my only desire is to get a better Act if possible. It is important from the practical and financial point of view, for, from any experience I believe that the difficulty is not in getting a railway charter but In*getting the money to build railways. In the committee, I am sometimes charged with being too liberal in the granting of charters. But we want railways in this country, and 1 "believe a railway charter is worth nothing unless it contains clearly, and in such a form us to be seen by the capitalists before whom it is put, the rights and privileges it purports to grant. As I say, I am prepared
to support any changes in the law that are shown to be necessary. I think it covers every thing that he mentions; if it does not, I am quite prepared to have it divided into subsections and change it. The old Act says :
This Act, subject to any expressed provisions of the special Acts and to the exceptions hereinafter mentioned, applies to all persons, companies and railways within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada except government railways.
I am the more mystified and unsettled by the language of this subsection divided into three subsections than I was before, and I am prepared to support the clause of the Minister of Railways and Canals, as he 1ms drawn it if he will show me any* necessity for the change. I think it is one of tlie first rules of legislation to use terse and comprehensive expressions. As the hon. member for Lincoln has said, there is less chance of the court attempting to put some construction on the elaboration than there was in the old system. I want the minister to understand that so far as I am concerned the bulk of this Act meets with my hearty approval. It shows a great deal of care and attention to the important and difficult subject of a railway commission, but it seems to me some of these general sections may have an application that we do not intend. But I have not heard a satisfactory reason why it is necessary to have this elaboration.

I had not concluded what I was going to say when my hon. friend rose. I am glad he is giving his attention to the Bill, because I know he will regard it fairly, and that his only object is to make it as perfect as possible. The hon. gentleman does not see why we should have three sections, where one was sufficient before. Moreover, if the hon. gentleman will look at section 5 of the present law. he will find there that several of its subsections have been dispensed with. Section 5 of the present law says :
The provisions of this Act, from section 32 to section 89 both inclusive, do not apply to every company and railway within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, but apply to

(a)	Every company whose authority to construct or operate any railway is derived from the parliament of Canada, and to every railway constructed or to he constructed under the authority of any Act passed by the parliament of Canada ;
(b)	Every company and railway to which such provisions are made applicable as hereinafter provided :
2. Such provisions shall, in so far as they are applicable to the undertaking, and unless they are expressly varied or excepted therefrom by the special Act, be incorporated with the special Act, form part thereof, and he construed therewith as forming one Act ;

3. Any of such provisions may be excepted from incorporation with the special Act by enacting in such special Act that the sections of this Act propose to be accepted, referring to them by the numbers which they bear respectively, shall not be incorporated with such special Act, which shall thereupon be construed accordingly.
It is quite a complicated series of sections and subsections that are practically rendered unnecessary by our including subsection 2 and subsection 3 under section 3.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As I said tbe other day, when you change your Act from tbe ordinary consolidation in tbe way I speak of, it is more difficult to get at tbe full meaning of tbe minister. It is a difficult thing to follow, I confess that.

Amendment (Mr. Lancaster), negatived, and subsection 2 adopted.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

No.
On section 4,
Where any railway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by a special Act passed by the legislature of any province, is declared, by any special Act of the parliament of Canada, to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, this Act shall apply to such railway, and to the company constructing or operating the same, to the exclusion of the whole of any other general railway Act, and of such other of the provisions of the special Act of the provincial legislature as are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Yes.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In other words, if I understand It aright, because it is very broad, it means that we are assuming that we have the right, and I do not dispute it, to legislate both positively and negatively, that we have the right to include by the mere declaration that it is for the general advantage of Canada the jurisdiction of any provinces that may have chartered a railway. To prevent any possible question arising we assume that we have that right ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has the hon. minister satisfied himself that there is no question about our authority to do that ? If we have that right I heartily approve of the section. I think the British North America Act simply gave the power arbitrarily to the general parliament by a declaration to undertake control of all these works. That has been the accepted idea and no question of doubt has been expressed in regard to it. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

What is intented by the Minister of Railways and Canals would be worked out just in the same wav. From the time the work is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada then you must



work out the corporate powers of your company in accordance with this Act, but it would not destroy anything that had been done before. Everything that had been done up to that time would be exactly as valid as if this Act had come into operation, but from the time this Act comes into operation you must observe the provisions of this Act which in so far as it provides for matters of that kind constitute the charter of the company in place of the provisions of the special Act under which it was originally incorporated.
On section 5,
This is a very broad provision and I do not know that it is not well but that we should have such a provision in a Bill of this kind.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Why did you put
in the words ' through-traffic ' ?
For greater certainty.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There must be some important reason for including the words ' highway crossings ' in this section. Under the old Act we always had by virture of other sections such power as was necessary. This section is to take the place of section 4 of the old Act, and it is in effect the same except that in this section you have added the words ' highway crossings and through-traffic.' The prima facie control of highway crossings devolves to the municipalities through the provincial legislatures, and the other sections of this Act sufficiently provide for crossing the highways. I do not say that the section is wrong, but I think we ought to know that it is. right because if we pass it without due consideration it might involve some jurisdiction over highway crossings that possibly would be ultra vires of this parliament. I would like to know from the min-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
ister whether the words ' highway crossings ' are necessary in this section, and if the matter has been carefully considered from that point of view. _

The inclusion of these words was very carefully considered by myself and by those who have acted with me in the preparation of the Bill:	The fact that
we must necessarily, if we are to euact a thorough la w, have control of the crossings of railways and the crossing of highways by railways, makes it important that we should leave it absolutely free from any doubt that we have asserted and maintained the right to exercise that power. It is a protection to the public; it is a sort of police power in one sense; and it is as necessary as almost any other power that we could give to the commission, in the interest of public safety. Nobody, I think, would be justified in claiming that this was the assumption of a power which could not be usefully and properly employed in the public interest; and the fact that we have the power to make regulations for the operation of all railways within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and everything pertaining to that, would put it also within our power to confer on the commission the power to regulate the crossings of railways and highways by the one or the other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may point out to the minister that he is saying, in the last words of the section, that the Act shall apply to highway crossings, whether otherwise within the legislative authority of parliament or not. If they are not within the authority of parliament, this Act cannot bring them in.
My hon. friend is in error in that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose they are not otherwise within the legislative authority of parliament, does not that mean that this parliament has no control over them ? This parliament cannot give itself control over them by simply saying so.

We would not have authority ns a parliament to interfere ordinarily with the public highways, but the moment we undertake to say that a railway shall be laid across a highway, then we have the power, incident to the exercise of our authority in regard to the railway; and every local or provincial power which conflicts with our power in that respect must be subordinate to it. For that reason, I think this language is quite proper in that connection.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not think there is any doubt whatever that these words should be in the Act. In that respect I do not agree with my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). They are placed here for

a particular purpose. It is well known tlint tlie parliament of Canada, in exercising its jurisdiction in respect to railways, undertakes to restrict people in the use of highway crossings. They are not allowed to permit their cattle at large on the highway within a certain distance of a railway. The parliament of Canada has no right to interfere with the people locally in the exercise of their rights over the King's highway except as an incident of railway legislation. Therefore when this provision is inserted in this Bill, it is inserted for the purpose of the railway, and power is given to this parliament for such a purpose whether otherwise parliament would have jurisdiction or not.

If my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is right, I understand that this Bill is extending the powers of parliament further than does the old law, which does not contain these words; and if the Bill is meant to give this commission authority over the highways, I am all the more against the section.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

one parliament has it, and in my opinion we have the right In connection with the railways to take it. If we do not take it, it belongs to the local legislature. The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. That was the intention before.

This House is of opinion that the tariff of customs duties should give such protection to iron and steel industries as will not only secure to our own producers and manufacturers Lhe Canadian market in articles now produced or manufactured in this country, but will also develop and sustain the manufacture in Canada of other iron and steel products which at present are imported in large quantities from other countries.
